content: In a study conducted in Korea, involving adults with diabetes with a mean age of 60 years, exercise interventions were compared to no intervention across 17 studies with a total of 425 participants. The results showed that individuals with higher baseline HbA1c levels experienced greater reductions in HbA1c following exercise. Aerobic exercise or a combination of aerobic and resistance training was more effective in reducing HbA1c compared to resistance training alone. However, no significant differences were observed based on the duration of the exercise interventions. Evidence was insufficient to establish a relationship between physical activity and the progression of complications such as neuropathy, nephropathy, retinopathy, or foot disorders. Strong evidence supports an inverse relationship between aerobic activity, muscle-strengthening activity, and their combination with the risk of disease progression in adults with type 2 diabetes. However, there was insufficient evidence to determine the effects of practices like tai chi, qigong, or yoga on these same indicators. A systematic review of 24 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 962 participants with type 2 diabetes (mean age 45–71 years) found that resistance training interventions lasting 6 to 52 weeks were associated with significant reductions in HbA1c compared to control groups. High-intensity resistance training showed greater effects on HbA1c compared to lowor moderate-intensity training. However, no significant differences were observed in fasting insulin or fasting blood glucose (FBG) levels across all interventions. Another systematic review of 39 RCTs involving 2,917 participants evaluated traditional Chinese exercises (e.g., tai chi, qigong, Ba Duan Jin) in adults with type 2 diabetes (mean age 59 years). These interventions, lasting 4 to 24 weeks, showed moderate evidence of benefits in diabetes markers compared to no exercise. However, no significant differences were found when comparing tai chi or qigong to other forms of exercise. A review of 13 RCTs involving 345 participants compared high-intensity interval training (HIIT) to moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) or no intervention in individuals with type 2 diabetes. HIIT interventions, lasting 11 to 16 weeks, demonstrated statistically significant improvements in HbA1c levels compared to control groups. Aquatic exercise was also evaluated in a systematic review of five RCTs involving 222 participants. Most interventions lasted 8 to 12 weeks. While aquatic exercise showed some benefits compared to land-based exercises or no exercise, the evidence was limited due to indirectness and imprecision in effect estimates. For people living with HIV, systematic reviews of aerobic and resistance exercise interventions demonstrated improvements in health-related quality of life (HRQoL). Aerobic exercise performed at moderate intensity (55–85% maximum heart rate) for 30–60 minutes, 2–5 times per week, over 6–24 weeks significantly improved physical and mental health domains of HRQoL. Combined aerobic and resistance training also showed positive effects on HRQoL, particularly in individuals receiving antiretroviral therapy. In terms of body composition, aerobic and resistance exercise interventions showed no significant changes in BMI, fat mass, or waist-to-hip ratio among people living with HIV. However, some studies reported improvements in lean body mass and skeletal muscle mass with combined aerobic and resistance training. Overall, while exercise interventions demonstrate benefits in glycemic control, quality of life, and some aspects of body composition, the evidence varies in strength and consistency across different populations and exercise modalities.
